extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate computer-science and mathematics students writing term papers and technical expository prose (and their instructors/copy-editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style, copy-editing, and expository-writing criteria for student term papers and technical prose (especially mathematics and computer science). Covers punctuation, word choice, notation, ordering of results, readability metrics, and copy-editing habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloaded or confusing notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't reuse notational constructs in ways that create ambiguity (for example, using Hj to mean Hi prime when Hi is already used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either write things out in words (e.g., 'each Hi is ...') or invent a new name; avoid crowding the page with too many symbols. If a notation clashes with other uses, rename to preserve clarity and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct genitive/possessive punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: When indicating possession (the genitive), include the apostrophe; e.g., "Hi's descendants" not "Hi S descendants".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for OCR/typing errors that drop punctuation; ensure possessives are formatted so their meaning is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens where needed in compound modifiers: e.g., write 'the one-vertex path' rather than 'the one vertex path'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphens prevent misreading of multi-word modifiers placed before nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer correct prepositions for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose prepositions that convey the intended spatial/relational meaning; e.g., 'vertex at distance d' is better than 'vertex of distance d'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small prepositional choices can change meaning or readability—check intended relation carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include spacing in inline references and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure proper spacing around references and punctuation (e.g., write 'using 4.3 (below) we derive ...' rather than '4.3(below)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spacing helps readability and avoids cramped typesetting; proofread for missing spaces introduced by typesetting or editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use results before they are proved (respect logical ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid citing lemmas or theorems that are proved later in the text, which can make the reader suspect circular reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure proofs and statements so that prerequisites are proved or stated earlier; make the ordering of results clear to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties/non-breaking spaces to prevent harmful line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typesetting ties to keep words or symbols together (e.g., keep 'e is' on the same line as 'e is').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent line breaks that interrupt or distort the intended phrase; for instance, tie multi-word technical phrases or symbol+word pairs so meaning is preserved across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous word senses and unfortunate coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware when a word can have multiple senses in the same text (e.g., 'left' as direction versus past tense), which can create ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternative wording or rephrase to disambiguate (e.g., 'the node is to the left' vs 'the node was left'). Watch domain-specific terms that collide with common words (e.g., 'planes' in aerodynamics vs complex planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequences of examples that build progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of examples that build upon one another is more useful for instruction than a set of unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design examples so each builds on prior ones, demonstrating increasing complexity or illustrating successive ideas (the Haddad and Schiffer paper was cited as a good example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Which vs. that: use restrictive vs. non-restrictive pronouns correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'that' as the defining (restrictive) relative pronoun and 'which' as the non-defining (non-restrictive) pronoun in expository prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: if you can substitute 'that' for 'which', do so. This guidance is intended for everyday expository ('shirtsleeve') prose rather than literary prose. Be aware that some established authors use 'which' in restrictive clauses, but many readers are trained by Strunk & White and Fowler—following the rule improves lucidity for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone matters: many tiny choices affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Small grammatical or word-choice decisions (such as choosing which vs that) contribute to overall tone, which affects readers' attention and commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate good small choices to preserve tone; frequent 'wrong' tiny choices can reduce reach and engagement. Use occasional conscious deviations when desired, but know their impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing exercises to build vocabulary, method, and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises like copying good prose, rewriting passages, verse-writing, or practicing rhetorical terms help develop writing method and a stock of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises are practice—some are more profitable than others. Copying and transforming texts, doing constrained verse exercises, and creating examples for rhetorical terms can improve stylistic control, but treat them as exercises rather than finished writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automated readability/style tools as prompts, not authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs produce readability 'grade' scores (based on words/sentence and syllables/word) and other metrics; use them to prompt re-reading rather than as definitive judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to minimize grade level moderately (Don's usual aim is to minimize level but not to overdo it). Interpret results in context: long musical sentences can score high but still be good; obscure field-specific prose may read as higher grade level. Use the tools to identify candidate problems to re-evaluate by human judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect style-tool diagnostics (sentence distributions, passive voice, parts of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style analysis can report average sentence length, percentages of very short/long sentences, frequency by sentence type, percentages of nouns/adjectives/verbs, and passive-voice occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these diagnostics to find imbalances (e.g., too many passives, too few adjectives); be cautious of odd classifications (e.g., program labeling 'It ...' or 'There ...' as 'expletive'). Don't rely on crude counts—consider rhythm and musicality of sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch flagged diction and questionable phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction-check programs flag words/phrases (e.g., 'gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to', 'very', 'literally', 'in fact') and invite alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider but do not blindly accept suggestions; domain-specific usages (e.g., mathematical 'due to' when attributing theorems) may be appropriate. Anecdote: authors often accept ~50% of such suggestions. Use flagged items as prompts to consider clearer wording (e.g., prefer 'because of' in ordinary writing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superfluous phrases and answer more questions than you raise
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate unnecessary words/phrases (e.g., 'he has heard', 'the reason ... is that'); ensure sentences supply needed information rather than creating vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase verbose constructions into concise alternatives (e.g., 'We remove the spaces because ...' instead of 'The reason for removing the spaces ... is that ...'). Ensure modifiers clearly attach to the intended noun (check 'fine' in 'fine book collectors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clarity, coherence, accuracy, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing must be clear, coherent, accurate, and—especially—concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is crucial even though it is hard: prefer shorter sentences when possible; cut unnecessary clauses and wording; employ rewriting to tighten prose (Pascal's maxim about longer first drafts is cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences and sparing semicolon use
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut long sentences into two short ones where appropriate; use semicolons only when clauses have a very close relationship—often a period is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semicolons can convey '19th-century mustiness' and slow pace; modern clear prose often benefits from periods. Use semicolons only when they enhance, not impede, readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long subject-verb separation and overuse of passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the subject near the verb (subject-verb-object style) and reduce passive constructions which make sentences harder to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many readability problems stem from subjects and verbs separated by long intervening phrases. Stick to active voice and S-V-O ordering where clarity is improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms and awkward technical phrasing in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use casual filler phrases (e.g., 'Anyway,' 'pretty straightforward') or clumsy redundancies (e.g., 'again iterate through') in formal expository prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose precise, formal phrasing in technical writing; conversational idioms weaken formality and may confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read your prose aloud to detect repetition and awkwardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading aloud helps spot repeated words ('this', 'they', 'just', 'then'), awkward rhythm, and phrasing that slows the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oral reading as a proofreading technique; it often makes repetitive or clumsy constructions obvious and easier to correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy-edit for focus, modifier attachment, and logical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: At the sentence-editing level, ensure focus is correct (the sentence's main idea is clear), modifiers attach to the right words, and sentences make sense (subject/verb agreement and semantics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop unnecessary phrases, fix misplaced modifiers, tighten subjects and verbs closer together, and ensure the sentence answers implicit reader questions (who/what/why/how).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of domain-specific usages when following general style rules
rubrics_metrics.description: General copy-editing rules (e.g., preferring 'because of' over 'due to') may conflict with established technical/mathematical usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a general-diction filter flags a mathematically conventional phrase, consider disciplinary norms and, if necessary, prefer the domain-appropriate wording, but be ready to justify it.
